title: Urinary Urobilinogen and Organ Impairment Predict Mortality in Severe SFTSV Infections - Bioengineer.org

analysis.time: The study was published on November 25, 2026, and the data analyzed covered patients admitted between April 1, 2021, and October 31, 2024. The publication date is November 25, 2026, and the event date is within the time range of April 1, 2021, to October 31, 2024.
analysis.location_and_population: The study was conducted across five tertiary medical centers in China, involving 798 patients with laboratory-confirmed SFTSV infections. The majority of the patients (87.3%) resided in rural regions.
analysis.event: A retrospective multicenter study published in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology reported that urinary urobilinogen positivity, elevated serum creatinine, and advanced age are independent prognostic markers of in-hospital mortality among critically ill patients with severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) infection. The study also identified hematological and coagulation abnormalities, biochemical evidence of organ injury, and urinary abnormalities as indicators of severe clinical trajectories.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Among the 271 critically ill patients, 137 died during hospitalization, resulting in a 50.6% mortality rate. The study found that non-survivors had greater organ failure and higher clinical severity scores than survivors. The risk factors included older age, elevated serum creatinine, and positive urinary urobilinogen tests, which were independently associated with fatal outcomes.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study is a retrospective analysis, and the authors emphasized the need for prospective clinical validation before these findings can be applied broadly. The research team included investigators from the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangsu University and Nanjing Medical University.

analysis.brief_en: A study published on November 25, 2026, in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology identified key risk factors for mortality in severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) infections. Conducted across five tertiary medical centers in China, the research analyzed 798 patients admitted between April 1, 2021, and October 31, 2024, with 87.3% from rural areas. The findings revealed that urinary urobilinogen positivity, elevated serum creatinine, and advanced age are independent predictors of in-hospital mortality among critically ill patients. Of the 271 critically ill individuals, 137 died, reflecting a 50.6% mortality rate. Non-survivors exhibited more severe organ failure and higher clinical severity scores. The study, led by Zhimin Tao and colleagues, highlighted the importance of integrating urinalysis with blood biochemistry for mortality risk stratification. However, the authors noted that prospective validation is necessary for broader application of these results.

title: Clinical Scoring Tool Distinguishes Lethal Viral Infection From Scrub Typhus Without Eschar

analysis.time: The study was conducted through December 31, 2024, with the publication date on November 25, 2026. The retrospective cohort included patients treated between 2013 and 2024 for severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome and between 2003 through 2012 or 2022 through 2024 for scrub typhus. The scoring system was evaluated for its diagnostic accuracy in these time frames.
analysis.location_and_population: The study was conducted at Jeju National University Hospital in South Korea, analyzing records from a cohort of 295 adult patients with confirmed vector-borne infections. The patient ages spanned from 18 to 92 years, with a median age of 63 years in the severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome group and 60 years in the scrub typhus group.
analysis.event: A retrospective clinical evaluation in South Korea demonstrated that a six-variable scoring system can accurately differentiate severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome from scrub typhus without relying on the presence of an eschar. The study evaluated the diagnostic utility of the Tick-borne Infection Severity Score across 295 adult patients with confirmed vector-borne infections.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome has mortality rates ranging between 10 and 30 percent, lacks established antiviral therapies, and poses grave risks of nosocomial transmission to healthcare workers exposed to infectious blood or bodily secretions. Scrub typhus, in contrast, has a case fatality below 1 percent and responds rapidly to empirical antimicrobial regimens such as doxycycline.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study's findings were based on a retrospective cohort and de-identified medical records. The authors outlined methodological limitations, including partially non-contemporaneous sampling periods and evolving diagnostic access. The clinical scoring tool was validated using a penalized logistic regression model trained on 16 variables, achieving a high area under the curve (0.989) and strong sensitivity and specificity at certain thresholds.

analysis.brief_en: A study conducted at Jeju National University Hospital in South Korea has developed a six-variable clinical scoring tool to distinguish severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by Bandavirus dabieense, from scrub typhus without relying on the presence of an eschar. The tool was evaluated on 295 adult patients with confirmed vector-borne infections, including 101 SFTS cases and 194 scrub typhus cases. The diagnostic system demonstrated an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.985, with high sensitivity (99.0%) and specificity (84.4%) when using a five-point threshold. At an eight-point threshold, the specificity increased to 97.2% and sensitivity to 90.0%. The study highlights the importance of an eschar-independent diagnostic method due to the biological limitations of physical examination findings. Cutaneous rash was absent in all SFTS patients but present in 70.6% of scrub typhus patients. The researchers also noted methodological limitations, including non-contemporaneous sampling periods and evolving diagnostic practices, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. The tool's performance was further validated using a penalized logistic regression model, achieving a test area under the curve of 0.989.
analysis.summary_en: A study conducted at Jeju National University Hospital in South Korea has developed a six-variable clinical scoring tool to distinguish severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), caused by Bandavirus dabieense, from scrub typhus without relying on the presence of an eschar. The tool was evaluated on 295 adult patients with confirmed vector-borne infections, including 101 SFTS cases and 194 scrub typhus cases. The diagnostic system demonstrated an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.985, with high sensitivity (99.0%) and specificity (84.4%) when using a five-point threshold. At an eight-point threshold, the specificity increased to 97.2% and sensitivity to 90.0%. The study highlights the importance of an eschar-independent diagnostic method due to the biological limitations of physical examination findings. Cutaneous rash was absent in all SFTS patients but present in 70.6% of scrub typhus patients. The researchers also noted methodological limitations, including non-contemporaneous sampling periods and evolving diagnostic practices, which may affect the generalizability of the findings. The tool's performance was further validated using a penalized logistic regression model, achieving a test area under the curve of 0.989.
